svg.title: Microscopy
svg.desc: MAGNIFICATION & RESOLUTION: Magnification: how many times larger the image is than the real object. Resolution: ability to distinguish two nearby points as separate. Enlarging a blurry photograph makes it bigger; better detail makes it clearer. Do not confuse image size with the amount of detail. LIGHT & ELECTRON MICROSCOPES: Light microscopes let you observe cells and recognise visible structures. Electron microscopes have much greater magnification and resolving power. Finer detail reveals and improves understanding of more sub-cellular structures. Improved resolution, rather than enlargement alone, reveals nearby details separately. THE SIZE FORMULAE: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. Image size = actual size × magnification. Convert image and actual size to the same units before dividing. Magnification has no unit; actual and image size do. WORKED MAGNIFICATION: Image width = 30 mm; actual width = 60 µm. 30 mm × 1,000 = 30,000 µm. Magnification = 30,000 ÷ 60 = ×500. Total microscope magnification = eyepiece × objective: ×10 × ×40 = ×400. Drawing magnification depends on the size of the drawing; it is not automatically the microscope setting. UNITS & STANDARD FORM: 1 cm = 10 mm; 1 mm = 1,000 µm; 1 µm = 1,000 nm. 1 µm = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m; 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m. Small unit → large unit: divide. Large unit → small unit: multiply. Standard form: a × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ a < 10. For example, 0.000060 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m. SCALE & ESTIMATING AREA: 20 µm ÷ 2 µm = 10: a tenfold difference is one order of magnitude. Convert units before comparing sizes. A scale bar represents an actual distance: compare the cell's image length with that bar. Use estimates to judge relative size or area when exact boundaries are unclear. For similar shapes, doubling length gives about four times the area; state the shape assumption. PRACTICAL: PREPARE THE SLIDE: Observe both plant and animal cells. Place thin onion epidermis on a slide with water. Use a suitable stain, such as iodine, to improve contrast. Lower the coverslip at an angle → fewer trapped air bubbles. Thin sample → light passes through; less overlap. Use a prepared animal-cell slide or a teacher-approved preparation. Handle glass, stains and biological samples safely. PRACTICAL: FOCUS & DRAW: Start with the lowest-power objective; focus with coarse, then fine adjustment. Centre the cells; increase magnification; use fine focus. Draw clear outlines in pencil; no shading. Label only structures you can identify. Include a magnification scale or scale bar. Use visible features to interpret images, not a memorised diagram alone.

svg.text: Lower gently → fewer trapped air bubbles
